speaker: The Chairman
text: Head I, Ministry of Social and Family Development.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government has put in place many schemes and services to support Singaporeans in building strong families.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The danger is that many may not know about these schemes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We tend to think that if people need help, the burden is on them to find out about the avenues available and whether they qualify.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They could, of course, come to see the Member of Parliament to seek advice and help.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But people who need help often are stressed for time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even if they had the ability, they would not have very much time to go through all the different schemes, let alone see the Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How can the Government make these services more accessible and streamlined, so that families are better supported, and can strengthen the bonding with their families?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To this end, I have three related questions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, for Singaporeans who for various reasons have no home to go to, what help can we render to such individuals or families?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How do we ensure homelessness is not an issue in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, at the Committee of Supply (COS) last year, the Ministry announced initiatives to strengthen social service delivery and provide more holistic support to those in need.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I must say I always find odd that our Social Service Offices (SSOs) are closed on weekends.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Would the operating hours of SSOs be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Third, social needs are growing in scale and complexity, and the social service sector provides many support programmes to help vulnerable individuals and families overcome their challenges.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How will the Ministry continue to ensure there is funding available to run these critical programmes?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In answering these three questions, I want to say upfront that I know the Government has many schemes in place already.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The deeper question I want to ask is: do people find the scheme easy to understand?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One of the most important actions we can think of when building a strong social compact in my mind comes from all Singaporeans sharing a universal dream, a dream of fresh possibilities, that if we are down and out, we have a chance to climb up and do better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But there are strings attached, as there should be.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Strings that means-test to ensure that the rich do not benefit from a scheme meant for the lower-income.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The 11th key feature says that 10% of the flats will be allocated to people who fall under a priority scheme.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is a link to the seven schemes – the Parenthood Priority Scheme, Multi-Generation Priority Scheme, Parenthood Care Scheme, Third Child Priority Scheme, Assistance Scheme (ASSIST), Total Points Scheme and Senior Priority Scheme, so, parenthood, multi-generation, married child, third child, divorce or widowed parents, tenants and seniors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And these seven then are multiplied across three different flat types.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I shall stop here because I think I have shown that the schemes are useful but also very complicated and not easy to navigate for anyone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This someone, let us call him or her, Officer X, could be sited in the community relations department of MSF or HDB.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Their home Ministry could be MSF or MND.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They should take as their model the information officers of the Ministry of Communications and Information where they develop domain expertise in housing matters but also speak to the specific needs of the Ministries and agency where they are sent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I shall say more about this in my cut on MND.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If anything, the Minister for Social and Family Development, who is also the Second Minister for National Development, is best placed to make this happen.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another area which I hope Officer X can help in relates to rough sleepers and homelessness.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is yet another example of complex needs, namely, people who sleep in public places, such as void decks or pavilions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some of them are not known to any social service agencies or had declined Government assistance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot force people to do what they do not want.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But prolonged sleeping in the public not only jeopardises their health and overall well-being.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It could also affect their ability to reintegrate and return to stable housing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What does the Ministry feel about this group of people, and what are we doing about the root causes of their resorting to sleeping in public places?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He said that he is the sole breadwinner in his family comprising him, his wife and two children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Comparing to his friend who lives in an HDB flat but with a higher capita income, his friend receives Government payouts whilst he receives none.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can we redistribute wealth more fairly and justly?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we ensure that those who genuinely need help get help?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Singapore evolves, as our population ages, as we become more educated and increasingly data-driven, how might our Public Financial Assistance system evolve, too?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the increasing availability of data, how would the Government use data to deliver public assistance in a more precise and personal manner?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As the local Member of Parliament, I hold regular daily phone discussions in a WhatsApp group chat comprising myself, my grassroots ComCare lead, the SSO General Manager, the Family Service Centre (FSC) social workers and heads of the local Senior Activity Centres (SACs).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Almost daily, we discussed families in need and nudged one another to join efforts to solve the problems of families presented to us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a strong need to strengthen our current social services delivery system in anticipation of these rapidly increasing needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The current Social Services Network delivery system needs to be extended and resourced further.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: MSO was started to improve the Government’s overall coordination and delivery of municipal services relating to estate management which involves currently more than 10 agencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is led by a Minister-level leader no less, and uses technology apps and data analytics to drive proactive problem-solving.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Annual resources are invested each year into MSO to drive productivity and template solutions for recurring problems.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I feel strongly that there is potential of a similar, albeit modified, MSO model in the social services landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Create a mother of all SSOs with mini SSOs in the network to lead and coordinate partners, such as the FSCs, SACs, HDB, the Ministry of Education (MOE), the Public Utilities Board, Town Councils and the Community Development Councils (CDCs), using technology, data analytics and the like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Will the Ministry of Finance allocate more funds to resource a stronger social services delivery system for MSF?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Now, all mothers are given the 16-week maternity leave, as well as a Child Development Account.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These enhancements show that the Government is prepared to make changes to support our young families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But because our single mothers also have less resources compared to a two-parent family, they would need more help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They face higher cost pressures in the child’s early years because infant care and childcare costs are higher than primary school fees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is when the Baby Bonus cash gift is timely to provide better care for our children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, even though many of our single mothers work, they do not enjoy parenthood tax rebates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These tax rebates can go a long way in meeting current needs and saving for future purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By providing the Baby Bonus cash gift and parenthood tax rebates, we are closer to being child-centric and more complete in our support to young families, regardless of family structures or circumstances.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first group of elderly who are doing strenuous jobs, such as conservancy work, collecting of eating utensils and cups at hawker centres, and trolley attendants.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second group, elderly who go around collecting empty aluminium cans, discarded cardboards or any other recyclable items which can be exchanged for cash.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The questions that many Singaporeans have in mind in relation to this issue are: (a) Why are our elderly who are supposed to be enjoying retirement in their golden age still doing such strenuous jobs and collecting recyclable items?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (b) Are our elderly doing such jobs because they need to do so or is it just a matter of choice?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Different views and perspectives have been shared on these issues, in particular, on social media.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some are of the view that these elderly want to have additional pocket money.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some mentioned that these elderly are doing so basically to occupy their time as well as to keep themselves fit and healthy, while many others opined that these elderly are in need of cash for their day-to-day sustenance.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The discussion on this issue has been surfacing from time to time in the past years, with some turning into an emotive one.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, Sir, recognising the root cause will enable policymakers to formulate more accurate and effective remedial actions in addressing this issue, assuming there is a need to do so.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, you can take your two cuts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First cut is on families facing multiple challenges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Challenges and issues experienced by families in need are never one-dimensional and often encompass a set of intertwining problems that cannot be solved in a piecemeal manner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An example of this would be a family with school-going children whose sole breadwinner has had to quit his job to look after a bedridden dependant.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under such a situation, the policy approach is to support the family with short- to mid-term ComCare assistance and to try and place the breadwinner in employment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to question, however, if this is the right approach because the breadwinner will not be able to hold on to a stable permanent full-time role due to the need to look after his dependants.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The children of the family are likely to perform less well than their peers in school due to the need to juggle school with caregiving duties when they are at home.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should adopt a more holistic approach to resolve complex social challenges individuals and families face so that we can help them get back on to their feet and to live a life of dignity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have a holistic intervention plan to help individuals and families that are facing a complex set of challenges?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can the Ministry help improve their life circumstances beyond just giving short- to medium-term financial assistance?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, social workers have come a long way since its early beginnings in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a more complex operating environment, changes in the demographics in our population, evolving family structure, income disparity and rapidly changing social environments, the training given to social workers needs to be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The National Social Work Competency Framework lays out the competencies at various levels of specialist knowledge.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It serves to define the knowledge, skills and attitudes required by social work professionals to deliver quality social work practice.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The competencies will also help to increase awareness among service users, policymakers and those who fund our social services and the effort of social workers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Framework will also help chart professional development and career progression.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MSF recently launched the Skills Framework for the Social Service, to help social service professionals plan their careers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can MSF further leverage this framework to drive and enhance skills development in the sector?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, over the years, I have encountered families which find life a struggle.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Major causes of instability include divorce, lack of finances and mental health issues that affect one’s parenting capacity and the ability to work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Children and youths in such families are subject to crises, sometimes on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They do not eat well and grow up with a maturity well beyond their years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is thus very encouraging that the Government commenced the KidSTART programme three years ago targeted at children from low-income families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are told that, under KidSTART, the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) coordinates holistic services for families, and monitors and supports child development from birth onwards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry elaborate on whether the Government is encouraged by the outcomes and whether KidSTART will be rolled out progressively nationwide?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will put us in line with the Convention on the Rights of the Child which Singapore has signed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, when is the amendment to CYPA expected to be tabled before Parliament?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, will there be any changes to the scope and resources for young offenders' rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, the digital age has revolutionised the way we live, work and play.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it is not without its dark side.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Young and impressionable youths are easily influenced by social media, sometimes going to extreme lengths to get more "likes" and "follows".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The presence of the dark web is also concerning if there is a lack of adult supervision and, sometimes, even with adult supervision.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Managing our youths' exposure to social media and the Internet is important, as they are the most susceptible to undue online influences.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Statistics recently released by MSF have also shown that cases of children beyond parental control have reached a 10-year high.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that MSF can look at how to better protect this vulnerable group, in particular, those that belong to at-risk groups.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can MSF provide an update on the committee’s work thus far?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, there may be emerging new types of homelessness in Singapore that are not about destitution and need for shelter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Destitute and Shelter Support Branch (DSSB) oversees 10 welfare homes that care for and rehabilitate destitute persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim is to provide a temporary place for the destitute persons to stay, where they are trained to become self-reliant so that they can return to their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the problem is that there are homeless persons who can care for themselves, who are practically self-reliant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further investigations by TODAY's journalist found that many slept on the streets not out of destitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They were homeless because they had personal relationship issues and were estranged from their families or because they were unable to purchase HDB flats or adapt to sharing HDB public rental flats with strangers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These homeless persons will not be amenable to being sheltered and rehabilitated in DSSB-managed welfare homes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Their sense of independence would be too strong and, in many ways, they are already self-reliant in the very struggle of keeping a job whilst sleeping on the streets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reuniting them with their families is a noble aim, but it will be necessary to provide dedicated counselling and mediation resources to achieve this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a need for MSF to study the homeless Singaporeans found on the streets today to understand these new types of homelessness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond understanding their homelessness, the aim should also be to redesign the DSSB's work to help return these homeless persons to their homes and families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Restrictions on international adoptions by some countries, such as China, explained for part of the drop.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But fewer unwanted pregnancies and higher abortion numbers have also been cited as reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe many Singaporean couples wishing to adopt would like to adopt babies born locally rather than engage in overseas adoption due to the risks, legal problems and medical issues involved in an overseas adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe many are also willing to pay for the medical, delivery and post-natal care costs for birth mothers as a gesture of gratitude and honour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there is an information gap that separates would-be birth mothers and adopting parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Single women with unwanted pregnancies do not have the full information available to make the proper decision to abort or to carry the foetus to full term for adoption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some may be aborting due to financial concerns related to full-term pregnancy and delivery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these reasons reduce opportunities for prospective adopters to adopt Singaporean babies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The promise of state support for medical, delivery and post-natal care costs will help bridge the gap.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Actually, to call the support "subsidies" may be wrong, as the costs can be clawed back through an adoption fee charged to prospective adopters who are willing to pay in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Needless to say, this will help boost our country's birth rates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I recognise there may be psychological implications and other issues for would-be birth mothers and prospective adopters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, this suggestion should be thoroughly studied with the well-being of the child as the central concern of policy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also would-be mothers who, due to very difficult and stressful situations, contemplate aborting their pregnancies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our organic total fertility rate will also increase.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Although much publicity has gone into releasing, especially the latest Third Enabling Masterplan (EMP3), not many people within or outside the special needs community know about it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Of those who are aware of it, many have no idea what is going on mostly, save the ad hoc good news that is coming out from the Ministry.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There are good reasons why the Enabling Masterplans have to be living documents, with regular reviews, reports and communications with all its key stakeholders, including the rest of Singapore society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: First, there is a need for the MasterPlan to incorporate the latest developments impacting the special needs community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Such changes may cover healthcare, housing and transport measures, for example, which provide more benefits or challenges to persons with special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Second, there is a need to update the Plan to take in new relevant ideas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Caring for the caregivers of persons with special needs is a good example.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The five steps are to identify, individualise, integrate, implement and inspect the caregiver support system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The response from the ground was favourable but how it is being considered in EMP3 is unclear.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Third, there is also a need to co-opt more people and organisations to co-shape and implement much needed solutions listed in the MasterPlan.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: It is much easier and sometimes more enjoyable to comment and criticise the system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But inputs are more realistic and balanced when the critics themselves also lend a hand at implementation, to experience and to help address the challenges of execution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We have The Purple Parade under our CDC; we have the See The True Me by the National Council for Social Services; and other awareness efforts by the Disabled People's Association and many other worthy VWOs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Surely, there is a way to stitch an alliance so that the overall and sub-messages on supporting inclusion and giving can reach out to more people more impactfully.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The overarching EMP3 may be a tad too general and there are some who cannot identify nor feel a sense of ownership in these macro strategies and plans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But the overall MasterPlan is a good launchpad to have different disability groups think about their own vision, gaps, strategies, solutions and seek more partners for their efforts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Hence, I seek not only an update on the latest EMP3 in this House, I also ask for a more comprehensive plan, both online and face-to-face, by the Ministry to regularly review and report to the special needs community and to the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Indeed, early intervention for children with developmental or special needs is crucial, and support that is customised to specific needs can make a whole world of difference.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is sometimes easy to put all children with developmental needs in one category.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But there are many different types of developmental delays – physical, cognitive, sensory and many different needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If an issue is identified early and targeted intervention is given, there is great potential for the child to overcome his or her challenges and live and function normally.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My son Ayden has Down's Syndrome and, as I was looking up for information about the ways to support him, I found many examples of people overseas with the condition who have excelled in different fields.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are those who are undergraduates, those who have given TedTalks, those who are sportsmen – many who are contributing members of the communities they live in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I want the best for my son but I will love him regardless of his abilities and achievements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is nice though to know that the possibilities for him and people like him are endless.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It all comes down to early support and intervention.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can we ensure that our children will receive the specific support that they need for different developmental needs?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If I may, please allow me to share three stories of my Clementi residents' journeys – three stories, three journeys, three questions that speak to policy and what the Government and society can look at.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of my Clementi residents, Ms N, not her real name, is a young lady with cerebral palsy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When N was younger, she went to a school for special needs students with cerebral palsy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But more recently, N has moved to a mainstream school.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She and her mum are proud of her achievement.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But as N's mother shared with me, it also brought unexpected challenges.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Previously, N's special needs school provided the transport arrangements.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But in the mainstream school, N discovered there was difficulty finding these specialised transport arrangements.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: N can take public transport, but it takes two different buses.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: During rush hour, some drivers will not wait for her and it can take multiple buses before N can find a bus to board.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when the weather is rainy, when it rains, it is even more of a worry for N and her mother.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, as more of our students with special needs make the transition to mainstream schools, we should look at how to maintain that continuity of support, so that the transition is not unnecessarily jarring.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I know our MOE and MSF colleagues have been looking into this, and I am sure they will continue finding ways to make things even better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can the Minister share about what progress has been made, what support is available, and how we can help parents of special needs children learn more about these programmes and how to access them when the children transition to mainstream schools?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr L, not his real name, is my Clementi resident.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He has been ill the past few years and recently lost his battle with cancer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She herself is not in good health and needs a wheelchair to get around.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They have a son who is nearing 50 years old, with special needs and a limited ability to take care of himself.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She says she hopes her health will hold up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But she is understandably worried about what will happen to her special needs son once she herself passes on.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can the Minister share about how we are coordinating across agencies and community partners to better support our seniors who are worried about their special needs children and how we can support the adult children when the parents become too ill to act as caregivers or when the parents pass on?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: During my home visits in Clementi, I have met Mdm T, not her real name.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But at the same time, the family has been worried about how to arrange caregiver support when the domestic helper is away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, Sir, these arrangements can be crucial to help prevent caregiver burnout, whether it is a domestic helper or a family member providing the care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can the Minister tell us what efforts are being made to make respite care more accessible to parents with special needs children, whether young children with special needs, or grown-up adult children with special needs?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, these three stories are of Clementi families whom I have met in the constituency which I look after.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we know these stories are not unique to Clementi.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And as we see through the eyes of our people, each story speaks to a broader policy question or a wider theme, a wider principle.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I look forward to hearing from our Minister on what we can do together – the Government, community and society – to help parents with special needs children, as the children grow up, and as the parents grow older.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: These numbers are expected to grow and, by the year 2050, almost half of our population would be above 65.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: One of the key challenges of growing old is deteriorating mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Based on a longitudinal ageing study conducted by the National University of Singapore Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, one in five elderly above the age of 75 shows signs of depression, and a Well-being of Singapore Elderly study led by the Institute of Mental Health revealed that one in 10 elderly above the age of 60 may have dementia.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Coping with mental wellness issues during old age is thus a growing concern.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: What support measures has MSF put in place to help those without mental capacity, particularly those with little or no family support?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, the Government has been encouraging people to sign Lasting Power of Attorneys (LPAs).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will encourage donors and donees to be more forthright and make any relevant declaration before they sign the LPAs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will also help to protect the LPA issuers in cases where donees may deliberately withhold such information when the LPA issuer is approached to witness the execution of the LPA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Failure to make the relevant disclosure should provide the LPA issuer with some protection in cases where the LPA is disputed by another relative or by way of adverse inferences drawn against, say, any donee with questionable intentions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The qualifications and training of the three types of professionals who are authorised to be LPA certificate issuers are different.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having such a clause will also provide further assistance to the LPA issuers in their assessment whether a donor is in a position to execute the LPA.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Brain development is highest during the first four years of life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The brain is forming important neural paths to help develop the child's ability to perform and function and learn well.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: One United States study showed that the quality of children’s early childhood experiences affects how well they learn; and the early years set the stage for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans have to adapt in this globalised and fast-changing world to stay ahead.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Government emphasises the importance of entrepreneurial spirit, a resilient workforce and lifelong learning to succeed as a country.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Our preschool is a good place to start to equip our next generation for this reality.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can we ensure that we develop our young's curiosity and avoid rote learning in our school education?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the preschool curricula, can we emphasise on unlocking creativity, inspiring curiosity, building character and igniting a true love for learning?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The aim is to meet today’s realities with tomorrow's possibilities.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could our Government facilitate more co-working places with childcare facilities to help young parents balance their working and caregiving roles?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially helpful for parents with infants and toddlers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government ensure that early education is accessible and affordable to all children and especially children from disadvantaged background?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How can MSF smoothen the subsidy application process and make it simpler?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: MSF mentioned better integration of social services and holistic support for residents.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: How will MSF ensure that children with developmental needs can receive the support they require?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The Early Childhood Industry Transformation Map (ITM) was launched last year by MSF.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What initiatives will MSF implement under the ITM to improve the productivity and working environments of operators and early childhood professionals?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, children from low-income families, like all other children, deserve access to high-quality formal childcare services and early childhood education.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, those in informal or ad hoc jobs may have difficulty meeting and/or producing proof of work due to the sporadic nature of their jobs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The current subsidy system incurs a high administrative cost.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A significant amount of paperwork and back-and-forth between childcare operators, MSF, parents and social workers are involved in appealing for the maximum level of further subsidies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The extra paperwork involved is often a disincentive for operators to enrol low-income children.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry allow all parents who earn less than $2,500 or per capita income of less than $650 access subsidised childcare for free, regardless of the mother’s employment status?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We, parents, are the best teachers for our children, and our home is the best school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And the most important time for us to be teachers and for our homes to be a school is during our child’s formative years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, our policies should not penalise parents who are not working so that they can be there for their child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government previously said that non-working mothers need less childcare but we need to remember that the fees for half-day childcare is not half of the fees for full-day childcare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not asking for families with non-working mothers to have more subsidies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am asking for it to be fair, for all childcare subsidies to be dependent on the household income and not whether the mother is working or not.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regulations should be enforced flexibly so as not to erode the viability of smaller centres that are providing good quality care.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are still learning things about early childhood education.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There should be sufficient space for innovation, research and experimentation within reasonable limits, to ensure minimum standards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are the contexts for my questions and suggestions which are as follows.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anecdotally, it appears that the pace is slow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, will children with high functioning or borderline special needs have their needs met in the remaining schools?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My assumption is that many boutique or niche schools have had to change their operations significantly to cope with the requirements of the new Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the Government monitoring outcomes on this front and what are the results so far?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, what is the situation for insurance for preschool centres catering to children with special needs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some insurers do not cover children with special needs, so preschools may seek to reduce their liabilities by not accepting children with special needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this something that the Government monitors to obtain regular independent assessments of early education outcomes?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the key strategies identified by ECDA is to raise productivity for the preschool sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Improved and streamlined work processes should be able to help preschool educators devote more time to care for children.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An idea in 2017 was the Smart Solutions rolled out by ECDA together with industry partners.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Comprising an integrated package of information technology (IT) solutions, I understand it is supposed to help with productivity at the childcare centres.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have these solutions helped to ease administrative duties, such as children’s attendance and temperature taking, parent-teacher communications and other work at the childcare centres?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another was centralised meal catering by the Association of Early Childhood and Training Services, ECDA and industry partners to provide healthy meals to preschoolers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More recently, there was also an e-procurement system to help preschool operators order commonly-used items from a curated catalogue of approved vendors selected.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Smaller operators can also enjoy cost savings through volume aggregation.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More importantly, it allows centres to free up time and manpower to focus on delivering quality care and development of the children.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have good tools to support our preschool sector to become more productive and, in turn, improve the working environment for the early childhood educators.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does the Ministry have detailed plans and timeline on assisting more preschool operators to leverage technology and tools such that the adoption rate of these improvement solutions becomes more pervasive across the sector?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Mr Chairman, the rise of dual-income families has resulted in many initiatives to ensure the provision of quality early childhood education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This, indeed, helps to cater to the needs of young families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: It ensures that our children start out on the right footing in their education journey, guided with the expertise from competent early childhood education professionals and committed operators.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Early childhood teachers are instrumental in spotting developmental issues in children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Above all, high standards in early childhood education allow for social mobility so that every child has a fair chance to succeed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: At the 2018 COS debates, MSF announced the launch of the Early Childhood ITM to improve the early childhood sector.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This will help provide more innovative services and productive processes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Measures have also been taken to ensure that early childhood is affordable and accessible to everyone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Effort is also being made to ensure the recruitment of quality early childhood educators.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: What initiatives will MSF implement under the ITM to improve the productivity and working environments of operators?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: What other initiatives will be launched to ensure the career progression opportunities for early childhood professionals to reflect the evolving complexity of their roles?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Recently, the Straits Times published an opinion piece from Katherine Mangu-Ward in the New York Times.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: She argues that in the quest for women's rights, a fixation on numerical goals can lead to a false sense of clarity and certainty.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There may be different views about the importance of numbers and setting quotas, but I think the point she makes about how we should not lose focus of the more substantive work of changing perceptions is important.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I feel that beyond setting numerical goals, it is important to get the whole community, men and women, on board to change cultural mindsets and progress together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The struggle by women for equal opportunities and due recognition has gone on for a very long time in human history.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Although there has been progress, there is still some way to go in addressing many issues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In Singapore, boys and girls have equal access to education, husband and wife are treated as equal partners in a marriage and, in principle, men and women have access to opportunities to work in various fields.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, we still see fewer women in certain professions and positions, we still see women leaving the workforce or struggling to juggle different roles, and there is some way to go to close the wage gap between men and women.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There have been various efforts to look at how to support and empower women, as well as to increase women representation in various fields.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: How can we meaningfully build on these efforts and encourage a change of mindsets within the community?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What other initiatives are there to champion women and empower them to progress?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Women provide critical contributions and a diversity of views.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is sufficient evidence-based data today to show that positive value that women bring on.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Even as we are an Asian Society, meritocratic performance of women must be upheld, acknowledged and celebrated.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Are there local data to support and show the improvements that have been made over the years?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank Members for their thoughtful speeches yesterday evening.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleague, Minister of State Sam Tan, will share more later.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: My colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim, will speak on this later.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: In the early days, there was a strong emphasis on self-reliance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Social assistance was minimal and community support was ground-up.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As our economy developed, we experienced uneven income growth.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We then introduced targeted social policies to give more support to those with less and placed stronger emphasis on collective responsibility and the need for many helping hands.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: As we face more challenges, such as an ageing population, shrinking family sizes and economic disruption and so on, individual and family efforts may sometimes not be enough.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: And so, over the last decade, we have shifted the balance decisively, with the Government and community shouldering a heavier responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We now have broad-based transfers and subsidies that benefit the majority, as well as more targeted assistance for the low-income, vulnerable and those with specific needs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: We have put in place trampolines to help people bounce back, in the words of Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, and social safety nets for those who cannot care for themselves and who have little or no family support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: But even as our broad-based policies and schemes and our targeted means-tested support continue to uplift many low-income families, we need to do more to better support families who are bogged down by complex and often interlocking challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: For such families, the consuming nature of their difficulties, such as addiction, incarceration, family violence, illness, divorce, mental health problems and so on, and often a combination of a number of the aforementioned, may make it difficult for them to access available opportunities, benefit from schemes and programmes or respond effectively to help that is offered to them.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: I know of a four-generation family where a teenage girl was raised by her grandmother.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: She dropped out of school, had a son out of wedlock a few years ago when in lower secondary.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The girl's son did not have any preschool education until recently when social services intervened.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Why is this girl looked after by her grandmother?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Because her mother has been in and out of prison for various offences – out for a while and now in for a long-term imprisonment for a serious crime.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Her father remains uncontactable for some time now and refuses to take responsibility for the family.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Unfortunately, her grandmother is showing signs of dementia.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, this is a family that faces very complex challenges which make it difficult for them to cope on their own despite many, many agencies and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) coming in to assist in different areas.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The question is: how can we support such families with their existing needs and also ensure their next generation has a good start in life?

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: At the Committee of Supply (COS) last year, I shared that MSF would be partnering and working with other agencies and community groups to transform and integrate our social services and strengthen that important last-mile support for families, especially those with very complex difficulties, so that help can be provided in a more comprehensive, convenient and coordinated manner.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Ms Denise Phua and Mr Seah Kian Peng asked about our progress.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) has also articulated the Uplifting Pupils in Life and Inspiring Families Taskforce (UPLIFT) proposals to support students whose performance and absenteeism are worrying.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: All of these that we announced yesterday carry the DNA of integration and coordination, a different way of doing things in the social services.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: So, let me now give this House an update on our broader level work across the entire social sector.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: This is, in a way, an interim report card.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, in the course of the presentation, may I display some slides on the screens for Members' better understanding?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They sometimes face issues beyond those that they are seeking help for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, if a family seeks help from the Housing and Development Board (HDB) because of HDB rental arrears, it could be because a breadwinner has lost his job and the family is in financial difficulty, hence, running into difficulties with arrears.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want to ensure that these families get the necessary information and referrals to the relevant agencies' services, regardless of which agency they first approach in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, even if they approach only HDB in the first instance and it is in relation to arrears, when the officer speaks to the family and understands that actually because of this and that, although it is beyond his remit and he assesses them for assistance on arrears, what he ought to be doing is to refer the family to, say, Workforce Singapore (WSG) or the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) to help the breadwinner with potential job matching and also to the Social Service Office (SSO) for financial assistance in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want each frontline agency in the community to be a potential gateway for families with complex needs to receive assistance from other social services, including those in the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They include our frontline colleagues from the People’s Association (PA), HDB, WSG, NTUC's e2i, Singapore Police Force, Singapore Prison Service, the Silver Generation Office and the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over time, we will expand to include more ground agencies as well as VWOs and community partners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Next, because the solution to families’ problems may rest with multiple agencies, one needs to make some adjustments before the other can give approval, families also need to travel to multiple touchpoints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And clients with complex problems are often asked to submit multiple documents or repeat their circumstances when they need help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We should not let this be a barrier to them seeking help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have, therefore, established a single touchpoint where they can access multiple services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some of our SSOs are already physically co-located with complementary services, such as employment assistance and family services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are using technology as well to provide some of these services via video-conferencing links.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: You can see that on the screen – a Social Service Officer working with a client, addressing the assistance that the SSO can provide, but also linking the client through video conference to officers in other agencies so that there is direct face-to-face contact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if the documents need to be shared, they can send it across.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is part of a pilot with the Legal Aid Bureau.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also observed that because agencies and VWOs are currently approached separately for specific issues, a family will approach HDB for housing-related concerns, approach SP Power Services for utilities issues, approach other departments for specific areas of needs, these agencies sometimes end up with a compartmentalised understanding on the family's challenges, rather than a holistic overview.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To address this, we are improving information and data sharing across agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have established protocols with HDB and MOE.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is work in progress and we will continue to expand these arrangements to more agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also using data and system interfaces to provide more coordinated and targeted assistance, especially if they can allow us to intervene early.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I agree with Ms Tin Pei Ling that data can be used to tailor assistance to clients' needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: SSOs and Family Service Centres (FSCs), for example, use Social Service Net to share client information with consent, and we are looking at the possibility of more information linkups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond systems and data sharing, there needs to be careful case coordination so that no Singaporean falls through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I assure Mr Darryl David that our SSO officers work closely with the family and other agencies to understand the family's circumstances and support them holistically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we take his feedback and we will seek to do better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, we need to better organise and coordinate all of this work, especially when so many agencies and VWOs may sometimes be involved in certain families' cases, so that families can achieve the best outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are, therefore, introducing a set of case coordination guidelines for agencies and case workers across the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Agencies will discuss and coordinate around the needs of each family, with one agency maintaining overall oversight for each complex case.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We call these Guidelines for Case Master Action Planning (Case-MAP).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Case-MAP will guide agencies and caseworkers from different organisations, both within and outside the Government, so that they share a common understanding of the entire family's needs and align their interventions accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if they identify barriers, gaps, roadblocks or inconsistencies in policies, criteria or operational implementation, these will be surfaced to the relevant Ministries through our SSOs to be looked into and resolved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The initiatives I have shared will strengthen our social service architecture and enhance the support which families with complex challenges receive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But going beyond systems, data and protocols, what we are really working towards is a strong, interpersonal network comprising our officers, social workers and partners across various agencies in every town embedded amongst our communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our fellow residents, VWOs and partners on the ground know the local community and their needs best and what local informal resources are also available to supplement formal support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Just imagine a map, each and every town in Singapore covering the whole island.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On this map, you can see many, many dots and each dot, from a planner's point of view, is a healthcare institution, a service centre, an SSO, a school, a polyclinic, all embedded in the town.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Each of these agencies is like a node that we seek to connect through the SG Cares Community Network.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These community networks seek to share and tap on the collective knowledge of the communities' needs, explore collaborations to make a greater impact, and to align and organise our efforts to better support individuals and families in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since May last year, we have started bringing together Government agencies, VWOs and community partners at the town level; not the headquarters, but on the ground, the people who are actually running the centres in the communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The second round for some towns will start taking place from later this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a follow-up, the SSOs will, in between each of these sessions, lead deep dives with relevant partners to tackle specific social issues, such as youth offending, disability, the needs of seniors in that specific locality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will also create more opportunities for our ground officers to build professional people-to-people relationships with counterparts in other agencies and VWOs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, when we talk about systems theory, we talk about silos, we talk about people guarding their turf.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: What better way to address this on the ground than to let officers meet one another and know that actually they are all aligned to the same purpose, the same families you are serving and let us work together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are already seeing positive outcomes from the networking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Secondary school students are befriending elderly residents living near the school, as well as in Thye Hua Kwan Nursing Home in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hope to see many more of such partnerships.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A strong network of support within the community is crucial for those who need more help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, ComLink and the LCN pilot, which I announced yesterday, will complement and strengthen support for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Imagine each and every town having an LCN, agencies, all knowing one another – whether you are in the Government, people sector, whether you are a religious organisation, corporates who want to come on board, informal groups who want to play a part – but doing so in a coordinated way through the SSO which understands the landscape, able to galvanise the data.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Each and every node in that town, with training, with kind of a relationship building, all aligned to say that, "Well, yes, I am doing my job.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in understanding my clients' needs, I understand the broader landscape of the challenges, and I will bring in my relevant partners to make sure we work together as far as possible." And within each of these community networks, you have your local LCN pilots, you have your ComLink, all working and plugging into the same motherboard.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The community support which I spoke about earlier, is also important to break cycles of offending for young people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Upon discharge from our MSF Youth Homes, young people may reoffend for various reasons – mixing with bad company, difficult family circumstances and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But every young person matters, and we will do our utmost to help them overcome their challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Jervin is a young man currently serving National Service (NS).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He was discharged from the Singapore Boy's Home last year and it is not easy to adjust back into the community after some time away.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Jervin's case worker understood this acutely and went the extra mile.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She checked in regularly on his progress for six months after his discharge, helped arrange his NS check-up for his enlistment and connected Jervin's family with the FSC for additional support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The social worker and I are both proud of Jervin, and we hope that he continues his good progress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Post-care officers in the community will, therefore, have a longer runway to build rapport and a relationship and help link young people to community groups, such as schools, employers, interest groups and other local community partners, to help keep them meaningfully engaged and envelop them with positive support and positive influence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if issues arise, they can help these young people manage and resolve them early.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The nature and intensity of support will be tailored to the needs of these young people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those with additional needs will be referred to partner agencies for support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, if you speak to youth work agencies, youth workers and youths-at-risk, including those who have emerged from a crisis, they will share with you that relationship is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you ask them to work with one youth worker in one agency and, say, the programme is over, go to another programme in another place and have another youth worker, that relationship is just very hard to rebuild.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if you push them from pillar to post and, say, there are multiple people involved, it will be just very difficult to break through that barrier, that wall that they put up around themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, this work of lengthening post-care builds on the work of the National Committee on Prevention, Rehabilitation and Recidivism (NCPR), and Mr Melvin Yong had asked for an update on this work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will help our youths reintegrate more smoothly into the community and reduce reoffending.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also strengthening statutory protection for children and young persons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the timeline of proposed changes to the age for protection under the Children and Young Persons Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are consulting stakeholders on the proposed amendments, some of which are substantive and we look forward to Ms Sylvia Lim's inputs as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is important to ensure that our partners are equipped to play their roles and that we do not unduly rush implementation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Both Mr Seah Kian Peng and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked about efforts to tackle emerging types of homelessness and different types of rough sleeping.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF works closely with FSCs, HDB and other agencies to coordinate support for homeless persons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh have pointed out, some individuals who sleep rough in public places may have homes, but do not, or are unable to go home for various reasons, such as conflict with family members, co-tenants and so on.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They may also not be known to social service agencies or have declined Government assistance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the year, we have stepped up partnerships with community groups who are active in befriending and engaging persons who sleep in public places, so that we can better coordinate and strengthen our outreach to them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Better understand the precise circumstances they are in and then allow us to work with the relevant partners, both local community partners, VWOs and Government agencies to try to resolve this challenge that they face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, what the House has heard earlier and, in fact, yesterday, in terms of ComLink and LCN work, was that the social services would play a bigger role together with ground Government agencies in a coordinated holistic approach to try to tackle some of the most difficult challenges that complex families face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By no means will this work be easy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this work will be intensive, and our social workers and VWOs will need all the support that they can get.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We cannot transform social service delivery or look forward to achieving this new social service landscape without our partners in the social service sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng pointed out, the demands on the sector are increasing and social needs are growing in complexity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we must grow and develop the sector to meet these emerging challenges and better support vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to provide resources, together with community partners like the Tote Board.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the years, the Tote Board Social Service Fund (TBSSF) has supported various social service programmes benefiting vulnerable families, children and youths, the elderly, persons with disabilities and persons with mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children (EIPIC) for children with developmental needs, FSCs for low-income and vulnerable families, and school social work programmes for at-risk youths are just some examples of programmes that have made a big difference in improving lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sustained funding is crucial to ensure that vulnerable groups continue to receive the support they need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It also enables VWOs to focus on delivering services well, and expand and develop new programmes to serve growing areas of need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This would benefit many VWOs who serve the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Beyond funding support, we must also support and upskill our social service professionals and develop their competencies to meet growing and changing social needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We launched the Skills Framework for Social Service in January this year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This helps our professionals to map out career progression pathways, and guides organisations in training and developing their talent in the social services.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Darryl David asked about further efforts on this front.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How can we better support our social workers and social service professionals to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I counted four but I still call it "tripartite".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They will explore further ways to build capabilities and strengthen professional practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes reviewing the entry and training pathways for our social service professionals, ensuring relevance in curriculum, identifying improvements for professional practice, and working on joint projects to strengthen evidence-based practice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chairman, I have spoken about our plans to provide Comprehensive, Convenient and Coordinated help centred around our community networks across the island, and also our efforts to strengthen our social service networks in every town and community, and to also strengthen our social service sector and professionals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We must commit to this if we want to better support and uplift the vulnerable in our midst.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we will work together with the community to do better, go further and make a greater difference.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But at the same time, we must continue to support and strengthen our families, as families are the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, now, let me address a couple of the cuts that Members have raised relating to family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if we could extend benefits, such as tax reliefs, to single mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Single parents comprise divorced, widowed and unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Most single parents are divorced or widowed and enjoy the same benefits as married parents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, all Singaporean children receive Government benefits that support their growth and development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some benefits, such as the Baby Bonus Cash Gift, tax benefits and housing benefits are intended to encourage and support marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nevertheless, we will continue to see how we can better support single mothers and their children who face challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Christopher de Souza asked if more could be done to support pregnant mothers contemplating abortion in coming to an informed decision, with the option of giving up their children for adoption instead.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The decision to terminate a pregnancy or carry a baby to term is deeply personal, and we must respect that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it is important that an informed decision be made.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Those who require further support will be referred to FSCs or appropriate helplines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MSF and the Ministry of Health (MOH) will continue to review how to strengthen and enhance the counselling process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Faisal Manap asked about working elderly Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Among those who work, some do so for financial reasons, others do so to stay engaged, some for both.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Retirement adequacy is a concern for the low-income elderly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have assistance and support schemes to ensure our seniors age with assurance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We regularly review these schemes and introduce new ones when required.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Much of this has been discussed yesterday at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) COS and more at the subsequent MOH COS, I presume.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Broadly, seniors receive healthcare support through the Pioneer and upcoming Merdeka Generation Packages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Silver Support Scheme and ComCare assistance provide further financial support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For seniors who continue working, they also receive employment support and assistance through the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), which has just been enhanced, and the Special Employment Credit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And there are options for them to unlock value from their flats, such as the Silver Housing Bonus and Enhanced Lease Buyback Scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If they need someone to kind of guide them, support them and link them to the relevant agencies, our Silver Generation Ambassadors and our AIC officers on the ground will lend the support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ultimately, helping our seniors age gracefully and with peace of mind is also about nurturing communities of care and support within their homes and community, from family members to volunteer befrienders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singaporeans need not face life’s uncertainties alone, and help is available to better support and uplift these individuals and families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is possible only with the strong partnership of individuals, families, the community, the social service sector and Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the essence of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Let us continue to strengthen the bonds that hold us together as we collectively build a better Singapore and a better social service sector for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has been working hard these past 12 years to challenge ourselves to become a society with bigger hearts, where all, regardless of age or ability, have hope for a good future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: This is what the three Enabling Masterplans are about: charting our direction towards a more caring and inclusive society, where persons with disabilities or special needs are empowered to participate fully as integral and contributing members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Members may well recall that we first laid the groundwork for an inclusive society by developing services under the first Enabling Masterplan in 2007.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We then went on to enhance support and services, under the second Enabling Masterplan in 2012.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Notably, we set up a dedicated agency, SG Enable, to support persons with special needs, and improved the quality of early intervention and education services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: It is on this foundation that we are continuing to push forward under the third Enabling Masterplan (EMP3).

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: Under EMP3, the Government is partnering the community to support persons with special needs and also their caregivers across different stages of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We want to give young children with developmental needs a good start in life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
text: We shall do so by ensuring that they have timely access to quality early intervention services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Mr Sam Tan Chin Siong)
